cells.tense: The practice is part of how you stay close to people now, and you're holding it that way today.
cells.ask: Ask one person a question you can't answer yourself, and leave the practice in your own hands while you listen.
cells.core:
Your work on yourself has stopped walling you off from people. The time alone feeds the time with them — you come back with something to give, and you give it without turning it into a performance. When a false idea about how you have to be falls away, you're not destabilized. It clears something, and you come back to the people in your life with more room for them, not less.

The practice doesn't need to get bigger or harder to keep this. It needs to point at someone. Pick a person and ask them something whose answer you don't already know. The answer arrives in their voice, not yours — and the practice stops being a room you keep to yourself.

cells.tense: You're working toward a version of yourself that hasn't arrived yet, and the not-yet is what's driving every session.
cells.ask: End one practice session five minutes before you actually want to, something still undone, and go be with someone.
cells.core:
The refining has stopped being something you do and started being something you owe. You're bracing against a future where if you stop, everything comes apart — and so you don't stop. The solitude that used to feed you now feels like the only safe place, which is its own kind of alarm. There's a cost to this you may not have said out loud: when you come back from that room, you're not really with people. You're still inside the next fix.

The hold you have on it is keeping something real in place, and it doesn't have to be loosened all at once. You can find out whether the world holds when you set it down. End one session before you're finished, with something still undone, and go be with someone. You'll still be here, still steady, and not on fire.

cells.tense: You're standing in front of a practice that wants you, and you're still taking your orders from an earlier closed door.
cells.ask: Put ten minutes on a timer and give them wholly to one small thing; when the timer ends, you're done.
cells.core:
You can still feel the pull of doing something steadily, of letting small work add up — and you don't move toward it. The hesitation has its own logic. Trying became expensive somewhere in there, so you stopped putting your weight on it. But the pull hasn't gone away. It shows up as restlessness in how you're with people — you want to be closer, and you keep the distance instead.

What's missing isn't effort and it isn't your ability to feel with people. It's a fair start. Put ten minutes on a timer and give them wholly to one small thing. When the timer ends, you're done. What you get is what those ten minutes actually felt like — not what the last time predicted they would.

cells.tense: You're already doing the work, steadily and well, and the sentence you'd use for it is that you're just like this.
cells.ask: Write one sentence about what your steady way of doing things is for — and if it's for someone, say who.
cells.core:
You show up to hard conversations the same way you show up to everything: prepared, patient, unhurried. That steadiness is doing work in your relationships right now, and you talk about it like it's a temperament rather than something you built. Part of why you keep it invisible is real — people treat you as the one who doesn't need anything, and that has been useful. But it means the thing you've made gets no owner, including from you.

What's actually there is an expertise that belongs to you. It doesn't need a certificate. It needs one sentence, in your handwriting, saying what all that steadiness is for and who it serves. Say it plainly once, and the practice stops being a trait you have and becomes a thing you decided to keep doing.

attempts.check: The draft leans toward assuming the person's solitude is a wound and that stopping practice endangers them — the record only establishes that practice has become compulsive and that isolation now feels necessary. A reader could reasonably say the refining is genuinely required by their work or their standards, so the cells must leave that open. The asks survive being wrong: finishing a timed session, saying one sentence before opening an editor, giving one half-day of full attention, or writing one plain sentence about what the practice is serving all return useful information even if the read misses. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any version of 'you've stopped cultivating' — it flatters the diagnosis and gives the person nothing to do today.
